nature-val-014.title: Net present value: future money in today's terms
nature-val-014.text: A lender might pay 99 cents today for $1.00 due in a month, but much less for a dollar due in 20 years. Money now is worth more than the same money later, because money in hand can be invested at once and start earning. Net present value turns that principle into a test for investments. Each period's net cash flow is discounted back to the present at a rate equal to what a similarly risky investment could earn. The results are added up. A positive total means expected earnings exceed costs in today's money, and the Net Present Value Rule says only such investments should be made. The method dates at least to the 19th century, and it has weak spots. The answer depends heavily on the {{ref:nature-econ-746}} and on knowing future cash flows, so sensitivity analysis is used to test it. When large costs fall late, such as mine clean-up and restoration, a high discount rate makes a project look too good. And it is purely financial, ignoring everything that is not money.

nature-val-001.title: Cost–benefit analysis: weighing gains against losses
nature-val-001.text: Is this project worth doing? Cost–benefit analysis answers by estimating the benefits and costs of a project, policy or investment and comparing them. It also ranks options by their total expected costs and benefits. The method follows a sequence. Analysts list the alternatives and stakeholders, measure costs and benefits, and convert them to one currency. They discount future amounts for the time value of money, so flows at different dates can be summed as a net present value. A sensitivity analysis then checks how firm the answer is. Benefits are valued by listing everyone affected and adding up the money value each places on the change in their welfare, in effect their {{ref:nature-econ-344}}. Costs are usually measured more fully than benefits, because market data on costs are relatively plentiful. In the 21st century, environmental effects are typically valued through the ecosystem services they provide to people, such as air and water quality. The tool is only as good as its estimates. Comparative studies find those estimates are often flawed, and interest groups may try to include or leave out large costs to sway the result.

nature-val-017.title: Shadow prices: money values where markets are silent
nature-val-017.text: Clean air has no price tag, yet a cost–benefit analysis needs one. A shadow price fills the gap. It is a money value given to something not traded in a market, or a market price corrected for distortions and social effects. Shadow prices are needed for two reasons. Externalities, costs and benefits that fall on people outside a deal, go unpriced. And taxes, subsidies, quotas and tariffs distort market prices. Tools for estimating them include contingent valuation, benefit transfer, hedonic pricing and the travel cost method. Lacking reliable data, analysts often build them from assumptions, so they are subjective and somewhat inaccurate. They are still widely used to value intangible costs and benefits, especially for public goods rarely bought and sold. Measures of a nation's total wealth use them as weights on produced, human and natural capital. That use is controversial, because little is known about how life-supporting ecosystems produce their benefits.

nature-val-019.title: The value of a statistical life
nature-val-019.text: Suppose 100,000 people would each pay $100 to cut their yearly risk of death by 1 in 100,000. Together they would pay $10 million for one statistical life saved. That figure is the value of a statistical life, a money value for avoiding one death on average. It values changes in the chance of death, not escape from certain death, so it differs greatly from the value of an actual life. Economists estimate it from extra pay for risky jobs, the {{ref:nature-val-097}}, from surveys of willingness to pay, or from discounted lifetime earnings. Each method can overstate or understate it. Values vary widely. Sweden's estimates range from 9 to 98 million SEK, and the UK put preventing a fatal casualty at £1.7m in 2013 prices. Philosophers such as Elizabeth Anderson argue that the wage data are unreliable, and that life and environmental goods cannot share one money scale. Both the methods and the idea of pricing lives remain disputed. Health economics more often uses the {{ref:nature-val-026}}, which scores quality of life from 0 to 1.

nature-val-008.title: Cost-effectiveness analysis: comparing without pricing
nature-val-008.text: Pricing health strikes many as inappropriate, and cost-effectiveness analysis avoids it. It compares the costs and outcomes of different courses of action without putting a money value on the outcomes. That makes it common in health care. Results are usually a ratio of cost to a health gain such as years of life, and the most common outcome measure is the {{ref:nature-val-026}}. A 1995 review of over 500 life-saving interventions found a median of $42,000 per life-year saved. For environmental goals with one physical outcome, such as cutting energy use, it can replace cost–benefit analysis with less labor. Climate economics prefers it when the benefits of climate mitigation and adaptation are hard to express in money. A variant, distributional cost-effectiveness analysis, also weighs how outcomes are spread, trading equity against efficiency.

nature-val-026.title: QALYs: counting years by their quality
nature-val-026.text: A year lived at a health utility of 0.5 counts as 0.5 quality-adjusted life years. The QALY combines how long and how well people live. Scores run from 1 for perfect health to 0 for death. QALYs gained from a treatment equal the change in health utility times how long the effect lasts. Weights come from methods such as the time trade-off or questionnaires like the EQ-5D. Combined with costs, QALYs give a cost per QALY, used in cost-utility analysis to compare treatments. The UK's NICE has used pounds per QALY since 1999. In 2018 HM Treasury set a 1.5% discount rate for QALYs, lower than for other costs and benefits, because a QALY measures utility directly. The measure is openly contested. Critics say it undervalues people with disabilities and the elderly and ignores how health is distributed. Oregon's 1989 Medicaid plan using it was found discriminatory. Supporters reply that with limited health budgets it allocates resources in a roughly optimal way.

nature-val-003.title: Discounting: how much the future counts
nature-val-003.text: How much should harm to future generations count today? Discounting is how cost–benefit analysis answers. It puts costs and benefits at different times on a common footing by converting them to present values with a discount rate. Net present value adds up each year's benefits minus costs, each divided by one plus the discount rate raised to the number of years ahead. The choice of rate is subjective, and for long-term projects it makes a large difference. A small rate treats current and future generations almost equally. A large rate, such as a market return, mirrors people's preference for money sooner rather than later. If long-run share-market returns are higher than risk alone explains, the equity premium puzzle, market rates would undervalue the distant future. Private firms often take their rate from models such as the capital asset pricing model. Critics argue that discounting biases the analysis against future generations and understates the harm from climate change. Scholars still disagree over whether, and how strongly, such effects should be discounted.

nature-val-006.title: The case against cost–benefit analysis
nature-val-006.text: Cost–benefit analysis adds up gains and losses without asking whose they are. That is the root of most objections to it. It rests on the {{ref:nature-econ-172}} criterion: a positive net benefit counts as decisive, whoever wins and whoever loses. As a result it can overlook equity and favor policies that help some groups while burdening others. Money itself is unevenly weighted. An extra dollar matters less to the rich, so unweighted willingness to pay gives wealthier people's preferences more weight. Time raises a second objection. Discounting may undervalue distant harms such as climate change and ignore the preferences of future generations. A third concerns what gets counted. Limiting benefits to economic values leaves out minority wishes, inclusiveness and respect for others' rights. Some writers judge the method unsuitable for analyzing climate mitigation as a whole. Supporters and critics still disagree on whether it can fairly judge policies with uneven or long-term effects.

nature-val-011.title: Multiple-criteria decision analysis: juggling conflicting goals
nature-val-011.text: Whether and where to build a nuclear power plant is a decision with very high stakes. Multiple-criteria decision analysis exists for choices like that. It is a field of decision science that weighs several conflicting criteria explicitly when choosing among options. Cost is usually one criterion and some measure of quality another, and the two often pull in opposite directions. When stakes are high, structuring the problem and its criteria explicitly leads to better decisions. There is usually no single best answer, so the decision-maker's preferences are needed to tell solutions apart. Ecological economists favor it as an alternative to standard cost–benefit reasoning. It has been applied to sustainability assessment, desertification risk and wind farm siting.

nature-val-016.title: Regulatory impact analysis: testing a rule before it takes effect
nature-val-016.text: A regulatory impact analysis is a document prepared before a new regulation is introduced, systematically appraising its likely impacts. Its central economic purpose is to make sure the regulation improves society's welfare, meaning its benefits exceed its costs. It usually compares different ways of reaching the same objective. The first ones are usually traced to the inflation impact assessments the Carter Administration required from 1978. Under Reagan, benefit–cost analysis became the required method. By 2000, 20 of 28 OECD countries required them, and virtually all OECD countries now use them; the World Bank has spread them to developing countries. The European Commission's impact assessments, introduced in 2002, weigh economic, environmental and social effects. In climate policy these analyses commonly use the {{ref:nature-clim-241}}.

nature-val-021.title: DALYs: measuring the burden of disease
nature-val-021.text: A pneumococcal vaccine in Gambia cost $670 for each disability-adjusted life year saved. One DALY equals one year of healthy life lost to illness, disability or early death. The measure adds years of life lost to early death and years lived with disability into one number. Each condition gets a disability weight from 0, no disability, to 1; Alzheimer's and other dementias score 0.666. DALYs are not a money measure, but costs per DALY can guide health spending. Like the QALY, the DALY is a health-adjusted life year. Harvard developed it in 1990 for the World Bank's Global Burden of Disease Study, and the World Health Organization adopted it in 1996. Before 2010 the WHO used age weighting and 3 percent time discounting, criticized for valuing young adults above children and the old. Critics also say DALYs measure productive capacity. Defenders reply that disability weights reflect effects on life in general, not ability to work.

nature-val-005.title: Cost–benefit review comes to US regulation
nature-val-005.text: Reagan's 1981 Executive Order 12291 made federal agencies produce regulatory impact analyses for rules with annual impacts above $100 million. OIRA reviewed them. Critics in the 1980s said the method could serve political goals, was biased against regulation and caused long delays. Clinton's Executive Order 12866 softened the test: benefits had to justify costs rather than exceed them. The practice continued under Obama. Analysts still disagree over whether cost–benefit analysis should be used in setting regulations at all.

nature-val-007.title: Distributional weights: making a poor person's dollar count
nature-val-007.text: A dollar to a poor person can count for more than a dollar to a rich one, if analysts apply distributional weights. These weights reflect {{ref:nature-econ-092}}. Without them, unweighted willingness to pay overstates gains and losses to the wealthy and understates them for the poor. Not weighting is itself a choice, one that in practice gives richer people a bigger weight. Weights are often derived from a Bergson–Samuelson social welfare function, a formula ranking outcomes for society as a whole. Another option measures willingness to pay as a share of income or wealth.

nature-val-002.title: From Dupuit's bridges to government policy
nature-val-002.text: In 1848 Jules Dupuit measured the social benefit of a road or bridge by adding up what each user would be willing to pay for it. Alfred Marshall later formalized the idea. In the United States, the Federal Navigation Act of 1936 required it for federal waterway projects, and the Flood Control Act of 1939 made it federal policy. Otto Eckstein gave it a welfare-economics foundation in 1958. In the 1960s it was applied to water quality, recreation and land conservation.

nature-val-004.title: Handling risk in cost–benefit analysis
nature-val-004.text: No forecast of costs and benefits is certain. Cost–benefit analysis handles that chiefly with probability, sensitivity analysis and simulation. Risk can be built into the discount rate, but it is usually treated separately, often allowing for people's {{ref:nature-econ-765}}. A sensitivity analysis shows how the result changes when the inputs change. A more formal risk analysis can use the Monte Carlo method, rerunning the calculation with randomly drawn inputs.

nature-val-024.title: Payback period: how long to break even
nature-val-024.text: A $1000 investment that returns $500 at the end of each of its first two years has a two-year payback period. That is the time an investment takes to earn back its cost, or to reach the break-even point. It is often quoted for energy efficiency upgrades, such as a compact fluorescent bulb, where the return is lower operating costs. Economists are wary. It ignores the time value of money, risk and cash flows after payback, so they prefer net present value or internal rate of return.

nature-val-018.title: Shadow prices in optimization
nature-val-018.text: A production line is already at its 40-hour limit. The most a manager would pay for one more hour is that limit's shadow price. In optimization, the shadow price is the change in the best achievable value of an objective when a constraint is relaxed by one small unit. Formally it equals the constraint's {{ref:nature-econ-455}} at the optimal solution. Every constraint has one, also called a dual variable. In optimal control theory the idea reappears as costate variables. Under {{ref:nature-res-221}}, the rent from a resource equals its shadow value.

nature-val-010.title: Pricing the energy that is never used
nature-val-010.text: Energy saved is never consumed, and such savings are sometimes called negawatts. {{ref:nature-val-008}} can price them in dollars per kilowatt-hour saved by an efficiency investment. The approach has a quiet advantage. It avoids guessing future energy prices, removing the main source of uncertainty in appraising efficiency investments.

nature-val-013.title: Evaluation versus design problems
nature-val-013.text: Multi-criteria problems split in two, depending on whether the options are listed in advance. Evaluation problems have a finite list of known options, each scored on several criteria. The task can be picking the best option, sorting options into ordered classes, or classifying them into unordered groups. Design problems do not list the options explicitly. They are solved by multiple-objective mathematical programming.

nature-val-012.title: Nondominated solutions: when no option beats all others
nature-val-012.text: When criteria conflict, there is often no single optimal solution. Multi-criteria analysis replaces it with the set of nondominated solutions: options that cannot be improved on one criterion without being made worse on another. From any option outside this efficient set, both objectives can be improved. On the set, improving one means sacrificing the other. The idea parallels {{ref:nature-econ-168}}. Maximizing a weighted sum of the criteria finds some of these solutions, those at corner points.

nature-val-020.title: The benefit–cost ratio
nature-val-020.text: Divide a project's discounted benefits by its discounted costs and the result is the benefit–cost ratio. It is a summary indicator, used most in transport appraisal. The higher the ratio the better; as a rule of thumb, a project is worthwhile when benefits exceed costs. Without a budget limit, the projects with the highest net present value are best. Under a budget limit, the ratio to constrained spending should guide choice. Long-term ratios, such as those for climate change, are very sensitive to the discount rate, on which there is often no consensus.

nature-val-027.title: The risk–benefit ratio
nature-val-027.text: People accept some risk for benefits, such as driving. When a risk is involuntary, they demand one as much as a thousand times smaller. The risk–benefit ratio compares the risks of an action with its potential benefits. Risk can be judged as real future risk, statistical risk from data, projected risk from models, or perceived risk. In medicine the ratio is a gatekeeper: research is considered ethical only if its risk–benefit ratio is favorable, as the Declaration of Helsinki requires.

nature-val-025.title: Project appraisal: should it go ahead?
nature-val-025.text: Project appraisal is a structured assessment of whether a project or proposal should go ahead, or whether it is viable. It often compares options using economic appraisal or another decision analysis technique. During the feasibility study it should weigh technical, economic, financial and social implications.

nature-val-009.title: The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio
nature-val-009.text: A new option usually costs more than the old one. Is the extra worth it? The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio answers by dividing the extra cost of one option by the extra effect it delivers. Cost-effectiveness is typically reported this way. In health care the ratio is compared against a threshold, often in money per quality-adjusted life year, to allocate resources. A 2006 review found that industry-funded studies often reported ratios below $20,000 per QALY.

nature-val-022.title: Dose and response: the dose makes the poison
nature-val-022.text: 'The dose makes the poison.' A small amount of a toxin may do nothing, while a large amount kills. The dose–response relationship describes how strongly an organism or biological system responds to different amounts of a substance or stressor. Plotted with dose on one axis and response on the other, the curve is typically S-shaped. The first dose with a response above zero is the threshold dose. Some cases fit a threshold model, others a linear no-threshold model, and some curves are U-shaped. These models are central to deciding safe levels of drugs, pollutants and foods, and often underpin public policy.

openers.cost-benefit-analysis: Should a new regulation go ahead, or a project be built? The standard way to answer is to estimate the benefits and the costs, convert those at different times into present values with a discount rate, and compare them. The method reaches into hard places: it needs a money value for avoiding one death on average, and money values for things no market trades. Health economists use measures that count years in perfect health, or years of healthy life lost. Critics object that the method ignores who gains and who loses, discounts the future too heavily and leaves out what cannot be priced.

reviews.cost-benefit-analysis: Cost–benefit analysis turns a decision into arithmetic: put gains and losses in money, discount them to today and sum them into a net present value. Shadow prices and the value of a statistical life supply money figures where markets give none. Every step invites dispute, from the discount rate to the way unweighted willingness to pay favors the rich. Where pricing an outcome seems wrong, cost-effectiveness analysis counts health gains in QALYs or DALYs, and multiple-criteria analysis weighs conflicting goals without a single money scale. Since 1981, major US federal rules have faced this kind of review through regulatory impact analyses.
